title: Which are matter?
stem:
Athe air inside a football
Bthe light from a torch
Cwater vapour in the air
Dthe shadow of a tree

Which of the above are matter?
key: Matter has mass and takes up space, even when you cannot see it. Light is energy, and a shadow is only where light is blocked.

options.text: A, B and C only
options.pick: Light seems to fill a room, so it seems to take up space.
options.why: Light is a form of energy. It has no mass and takes up no space.

options.text: A and C only
options.pick: Check each one: does it have mass, and does it take up space?
options.why: Air and water vapour are gases. They have mass and take up space, so they are matter. Light is energy, and a shadow is only where light is blocked.

options.text: C only
options.pick: Water vapour is water, which is clearly matter, but air seems to be nothing.
options.why: The air in the football has mass (a pumped-up ball is heavier) and takes up space, so it is matter.

options.text: A, C and D only
options.pick: A shadow has a shape and a size you can see.
options.why: A shadow is not stuff. It is the area where light is blocked, so it has no mass.

title: Pouring juice
stem:
Ali pours 200 mL of juice from a tall, narrow glass into a wide, shallow bowl.

Which statement is correct?
key: A liquid takes the shape of its container, but its volume stays the same.

options.text: The volume becomes less, because the level in the bowl is lower.
options.pick: The level drops a lot, so it looks like there is less juice.
options.why: The level is lower because the juice is spread over a wider area. There is still 200 mL.

options.text: The juice keeps both its shape and its volume.
options.pick: Pouring does not seem to change the juice itself.
options.why: A liquid has no definite shape: it takes the shape of the bowl.

options.text: The volume becomes more, because the juice spreads out further.
options.pick: It covers more of the bowl, so it seems bigger.
options.why: Spreading out changes the shape, not the volume.

options.text: The juice changes shape, but its volume stays 200 mL.
options.pick: Ask what changed when the juice moved: its shape, its amount, or both?
options.why: A liquid takes the shape of its container but has a definite volume. Nothing was added or lost.

title: Is sand a solid?
stem:
Sand can be poured, and it takes the shape of the container it is poured into.

Why is sand still a solid?
key: Judge a powder by a single grain, not by the heap. Each grain keeps its own shape and volume.

options.text: Each grain of sand has a definite shape and a definite volume.
options.pick: Look closely at one grain instead of the whole heap.
options.why: The heap takes the container's shape only because the grains slide past one another. Each grain keeps its own shape and volume.

options.text: It is not. Sand is a liquid because it can be poured.
options.pick: Things that pour, like water, are liquids.
options.why: Pouring is not the test. Each grain keeps its own shape and volume, which no liquid does.

options.text: Sand is a solid only when it is wet and sticks together.
options.pick: Wet sand holds a shape, like a sandcastle, so it seems solid only then.
options.why: Dry sand is a solid too. Each grain has a definite shape and volume, wet or dry.

options.text: Sand is a solid because it has mass.
options.pick: Solids feel like they have a fixed amount of stuff.
options.why: Liquids and gases have mass too. Sand is a solid because each grain has a definite shape and volume.

title: Three sealed syringes
stem:
Three identical sealed syringes, P, Q and R, each contain either air, water, or a block of wax that fills the syringe. When each plunger is pushed, only P's plunger moves in.

Which statement is correct?
key: Only a gas can be squashed into less space, and even a gas never takes up no space.

options.text: P contains water.
options.pick: Water flows easily, so it seems it would let the plunger move.
options.why: Water flows, but it has a definite volume and cannot be squashed.

options.text: P contains the wax.
options.pick: Wax is soft, so it seems squashable.
options.why: The wax fills the syringe and has a definite volume, so it cannot be squashed into less space.

options.text: P contains air. Its plunger moves in part of the way.
options.pick: Which state has no definite volume?
options.why: A gas can be squashed into less space, but it still takes up space and pushes back, so the plunger stops part of the way.

options.text: P contains air. Its plunger can be pushed all the way to the end.
options.pick: Air is easy to squash, so it seems it could be squashed away completely.
options.why: Air can be squashed into less space, but never into no space.

title: The volume of a stone
stem:
A measuring cylinder contains 50 mL of water. A stone is lowered in, and the water level rises to 72 mL.

What is the volume of the stone? (1 mL = 1 cm³)
figure: <svg viewBox='0 0 360 236' role='img' aria-label='Two measuring cylinders. Before: water at 50 mL. After the stone is lowered in: water at 72 mL.'><rect class='fa' x='72' y='120' width='46' height='88'/><path class='ln' d='M70 24 V210 H120 V24'/><path class='ln' d='M60 214 H130'/><path class='ln' style='stroke-width:1.5' d='M112 192 H120 M112 174 H120 M112 156 H120 M112 138 H120 M112 120 H120 M112 102 H120 M112 84 H120 M112 66 H120 M112 48 H120 M112 30 H120'/><path class='ln' d='M120 120 H140'/><text class='lbl' x='144' y='124'>50 mL</text><text class='lbl' x='95' y='230' text-anchor='middle'>Before</text><rect class='fa' x='232' y='80' width='46' height='128'/><path class='sl' d='M240 206 l6 -16 l18 -6 l14 8 l-4 14 z'/><path class='ln' d='M230 24 V210 H280 V24'/><path class='ln' d='M220 214 H290'/><path class='ln' style='stroke-width:1.5' d='M272 192 H280 M272 174 H280 M272 156 H280 M272 138 H280 M272 120 H280 M272 102 H280 M272 84 H280 M272 66 H280 M272 48 H280 M272 30 H280'/><path class='ln' d='M280 80 H300'/><text class='lbl' x='304' y='84'>72 mL</text><text class='lbl' x='255' y='230' text-anchor='middle'>After</text></svg>
key: Volume of the stone = level after − level before.

options.text: 72 cm³
options.pick: 72 is the reading with the stone in it.
options.why: 72 mL is the water and the stone together. Subtract the 50 mL of water.

options.text: 122 cm³
options.pick: Both numbers seem to belong in the answer, so add them.
options.why: The stone's volume is the change in the level, so subtract.

options.text: 50 cm³
options.pick: 50 mL is the first reading, so it seems to be the measurement.
options.why: 50 mL is the water before the stone went in. It says nothing about the stone.

options.text: 22 cm³
options.pick: The stone pushed the water up. Subtract: 72 − 50.
options.why: The rise in the level equals the space the stone takes up: 22 mL, which is 22 cm³.

title: Finding the mass of a stone
stem: Which apparatus should be used to measure the mass of a stone?
key: Mass: electronic balance (g, kg). Volume: measuring cylinder (mL, cm³).

options.text: A measuring cylinder with water
options.pick: You have seen stones put into measuring cylinders in class.
options.why: That finds the stone's volume (the space it takes up), not its mass.

options.text: An electronic balance
options.pick: Mass is found by weighing.
options.why: An electronic balance measures mass in g or kg.

options.text: A ruler
options.pick: Measuring the stone's size seems to tell you how much there is.
options.why: A ruler measures length. Size does not tell you mass.

options.text: A beaker
options.pick: Beakers are used for measuring in the lab.
options.why: A beaker only roughly measures the volume of a liquid. It cannot measure mass.

title: A big balloon and a small marble
stem:
A balloon blown up with air is much bigger than a glass marble.

Which statement is correct?
key: Volume is the space something takes up. Size tells you nothing certain about mass.

options.text: The balloon has a greater mass because it is bigger.
options.pick: Bigger things are usually heavier.
options.why: Size tells you volume, not mass. You would need a balance to compare their masses.

options.text: The balloon has no mass because it is filled with air.
options.pick: Balloons float about, so they seem to weigh nothing.
options.why: The rubber and the air inside both have mass. It is just small.

options.text: The balloon takes up more space than the marble.
options.pick: Bigger means more volume. Ask what size alone can tell you.
options.why: Volume is the space something takes up, so the bigger balloon has the greater volume. Its size tells you nothing certain about its mass.

options.text: The marble takes up more space because it is heavier.
options.pick: Heavier things seem to be bigger.
options.why: Mass and volume are different. Being heavier does not make something take up more space.

title: Where does the gas go?
stem:
Some coloured gas is released into one corner of a closed glass box.

After some time, where is the coloured gas?
key: A gas has no definite shape or volume. It spreads out to fill its whole container.

options.text: Spread out through the whole box
options.pick: A gas has no definite shape or volume.
options.why: A gas spreads out to fill the whole of its container.

options.text: Lying on the bottom of the box, like a liquid
options.pick: Liquids settle at the bottom, so gases seem to as well.
options.why: A liquid has a definite volume and collects at the bottom. A gas fills the whole box.

options.text: Still in the corner where it was released
options.pick: Nothing pushed it, so it seems to stay put.
options.why: A gas does not keep its shape or stay in one place.

options.text: Gone, because a gas takes up no space
options.pick: The colour may be harder to see later.
options.why: Gas is matter and takes up space. The colour fades only because the gas has spread out.

title: A fair test with balloons
stem:
Ravi wants to show that air has mass. He hangs two balloons at the two ends of a stick and balances it. Then he lets the air out of one balloon.

What must be the same about the two balloons at the start?
key: In a fair test only one thing differs. Here it is whether a balloon still has its air.

options.text: They must be different colours so they can be told apart.
options.pick: It is easy to keep track of them that way.
options.why: Colour has no effect on the balance, so it is not something that needs controlling.

options.text: They must be the same kind, blown up the same amount, and hung at the same distance from the middle.
options.pick: The only difference allowed is whether a balloon still has its air.
options.why: If anything else differs, the stick could tip because of that, not because of the air.

options.text: Only their distance from the middle must be the same. Their size does not matter.
options.pick: The distance from the middle obviously matters for balancing.
options.why: A bigger balloon holds more air and more rubber. Different sizes would spoil the test.

options.text: Nothing needs to be the same, because air has no mass anyway.
options.pick: Air feels weightless, so the test seems pointless.
options.why: The stick does tip when one balloon loses its air. That is the evidence that air has mass.

title: Which are solids?
stem:
Asugar
Bflour
Ccooking oil
Dice

Which of the above are solids?
key: A solid keeps its own definite shape and volume. For a powder, look at one grain.

options.text: D only
options.pick: Sugar and flour can be poured, so they seem to be liquids.
options.why: Each grain keeps its own definite shape and volume, so powders are solids.

options.text: A and B only
options.pick: Ice melts into water, so it seems to be a liquid.
options.why: Ice is water in its solid state. While it is ice, it has a definite shape and volume.

options.text: A, B, C and D
options.pick: Cooking oil is thick, so it seems solid.
options.why: Oil takes the shape of its container, so it is a liquid.

options.text: A, B and D only
options.pick: Check each one: does it keep its own definite shape and volume?
options.why: Each sugar crystal and flour grain keeps its own shape and volume, and so does ice. Oil takes the shape of its container.

title: Sugar in a jar
stem:
Sugar takes the shape of the jar it is poured into.

Why is it still a solid?
key: Judge a powder by one crystal, not the heap.

options.text: Each crystal keeps its own definite shape and volume.
options.pick: Look at one crystal instead of the whole heap.
options.why: The heap takes the jar's shape only because the crystals slide past one another. Each crystal keeps its own shape and volume.

options.text: It is a liquid, because it takes the shape of the jar.
options.pick: Liquids take the shape of their container, and so does the sugar.
options.why: Taking the container's shape is not the test for a powder. Each crystal keeps its own shape and volume, which no liquid does.

options.text: It is a gas, because it spreads across the bottom of the jar.
options.pick: The sugar spreads out to cover the bottom.
options.why: A gas fills the whole container. Sugar settles at the bottom, and each crystal keeps its shape and volume.

options.text: It is a solid only when it is in a lump.
options.pick: A sugar cube clearly holds its shape, but loose sugar does not.
options.why: Loose sugar is a solid too. Each crystal has a definite shape and volume, whether in a lump or loose.

title: The overflowing container
stem:
A container is filled with water to the brim. When a stone is lowered in, 35 mL of water overflows into a measuring cylinder.

What is the volume of the stone?
key: The water pushed out equals the space the stone takes up.

options.text: The volume of the water left in the container
options.pick: That is the other water reading, so it seems to be the answer.
options.why: The water left behind tells you nothing about the stone. The overflow does.

options.text: It cannot be found without the stone's mass
options.pick: Measuring a stone usually seems to mean weighing it.
options.why: Volume is found from the water pushed out. Mass is not needed.

options.text: 35 cm³
options.pick: The stone pushed some water out. How much space did it need?
options.why: The stone pushed out exactly as much water as the space it takes up: 35 mL, which is 35 cm³.

options.pick: The number 35 is right, and grams are a familiar unit.
options.why: The overflow measures volume, in mL or cm³. Grams measure mass.

title: Two stones
stem:
Two stones, X and Y, were lowered into two measuring cylinders of water. The readings are shown.

Which stone has the bigger volume?
figure:
StoneWater level before (mL)Water level after (mL)
X3048
Y5064
key: Compare the rise in water level, not the final reading.

options.text: Y, because its water level ended higher
options.pick: 64 mL is the highest reading.
options.why: Y's cylinder started with more water. Only the rise counts: Y's is 14 mL, smaller than X's 18 mL.

options.text: They are the same, because both made the water rise
options.pick: Both stones pushed the water up.
options.why: They pushed it up by different amounts: 18 mL and 14 mL.

options.text: It cannot be told without weighing them
options.pick: Comparing stones seems to need their masses.
options.why: Volume comes from the rise in water level. Weighing gives mass, which is a different quantity.

options.text: X: 18 cm³ compared with 14 cm³
options.pick: Work out the rise for each stone: 48 − 30 and 64 − 50.
options.why: X raised the water by 18 mL and Y by 14 mL, so X takes up more space.

title: Taking up the same space
stem:
A stone and a bag of feathers take up the same amount of space.

Which statement is correct?
key: The same volume does not mean the same mass.

options.text: They must have the same mass.
options.pick: Things the same size seem to weigh the same.
options.why: The same volume does not mean the same mass. You would need a balance to compare.

options.text: They have the same volume, but their masses may be different.
options.pick: "Same space" tells you about volume. Does it tell you about mass?
options.why: Taking up the same space means the same volume. Mass is a separate measurement and can be very different.

options.text: The feathers have no mass.
options.pick: Feathers feel weightless.
options.why: Feathers are matter, so they have mass. It is just small.

options.text: They have the same mass and volume because both are solids.
options.pick: Being in the same state seems to make them alike.
options.why: Solids can have very different masses for the same volume. The state does not decide the mass.

title: Mass and volume of a toy car
stem: Which apparatus should be used to find the mass and the volume of a small toy car that sinks in water?
key: Mass: electronic balance. Volume of an odd-shaped object that sinks: rise in water in a measuring cylinder.

options.pick: Both pieces of apparatus are right for the toy car, so the order seems not to matter.
options.why: They are swapped. A measuring cylinder finds volume, and a balance finds mass.

options.pick: A ruler measures the car's size, which seems to show how much there is.
options.why: A ruler measures length, not mass. And a balance cannot find volume.

options.pick: Mass is found by weighing. The volume of an odd-shaped object is found by displacement.
options.why: A balance gives the mass. The rise in water in a measuring cylinder gives the volume.

options.pick: A balance shows a number for anything you put on it.
options.why: A balance measures mass only. Volume needs the measuring cylinder.

title: Milk in a tall glass
stem:
150 mL of milk is poured from a carton into a tall, narrow glass, and the level looks high.

What is the volume of the milk now?
key: A liquid has a definite volume. Pouring changes its shape, not its volume.

options.text: 150 mL
options.pick: Nothing was added or spilled. What changed?
options.why: A liquid has a definite volume. Only its shape changed, so it is still 150 mL.

options.text: More than 150 mL, because the level is higher
options.pick: A higher level looks like more milk.
options.why: The level is higher because the glass is narrow. The volume has not changed.

options.text: Less than 150 mL, because the glass is narrower
options.pick: A narrow glass seems to hold less.
options.why: The milk is squeezed into a taller shape, not a smaller amount. It is still 150 mL.

options.text: It cannot be known without measuring its mass
options.pick: Checking an amount seems to need a balance.
options.why: Volume is not found from mass. Nothing was added or lost, so the volume is still 150 mL.
